def: Removing the thin outer skin of the sesame seed so the inside is white and mild. The seed without skin is called hulled sesame.
Sesame seed with its outer skin removed. Whiter and milder; used for tahini, halawa and bread toppings.
Sesame seed as it comes from the farm, cleaned but with its skin still on.
A paste made by roasting and grinding hulled sesame. Used in hummus, sauces and halawa.
A sweet made from tahini and sugar (also spelled halva).
Something left over when making the main product (skins, broken seeds, fibre). It can often be sold for extra income.
A set of machines in the factory that turns one input into one main product, step by step.
Money left from each tonne sold after paying for raw material and processing, before office and staff costs.
The sales volume at which income exactly covers all costs. Below it you lose money, above it you make profit.
Money spent once on machines, buildings and installation (capital expenditure).
Cash tied up in stock and unpaid customer invoices, needed to keep the business running.
How much finished product you get from one tonne of raw material, as a percentage.
Paying another factory to process your raw material for you, instead of owning machines.
Making a product that a supermarket sells under its own brand name.
'Free On Board': the price of goods loaded on the ship at the seller's port. The buyer pays sea freight from there.
Total cost of goods once they reach your factory: purchase price plus shipping, insurance, port fees and trucking.
1,000 kilograms (one metric ton).
A standard steel shipping box. A 20-foot container holds about 18–19 tonnes of seed.
A customs area where imported goods can be stored and processed without paying import duty, as long as they are re-exported.
Special Economic Zone: an area with lighter rules, tax and customs benefits to attract industry (e.g. Jazan).
Selling abroad goods that were imported and processed in the country.
Getting imported goods officially released by customs (ZATCA in Saudi Arabia) after checking documents and paying any duty.
Saudi Food and Drug Authority. Licenses food factories and checks imported food.
Certification that food meets Islamic dietary rules. Required for the Saudi and GCC markets.
An international food-safety certificate for factories. Big food buyers ask for it.
A food-safety certificate widely demanded by UK and EU supermarkets.
Bacteria that can cause food poisoning. The main safety test for sesame.
A natural poison made by mould on badly dried crops like peanuts and seeds. Strictly limited by law.
Maximum amount of farm-chemical residue allowed in food. The EU's limits are among the strictest.
Treating the product with hot steam for a short time to kill bacteria without cooking it.
A machine with cameras that blows out dark or damaged seeds with air jets.
Government document confirming plant products are free of pests and diseases. Needed to export crops.
Document stating which country the goods come from. Affects import duty.
Sudanese Standards and Metrology Organization: checks export quality in Sudan.
An independent company (e.g. SGS, Bureau Veritas) checks quality and weight before goods are loaded.
Grain and Feed Trade Association: standard international contract rules for trading crops. (Also the name of the Arab free-trade area.)
Gulf Cooperation Council: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain.
Goods count as 'Made in Saudi' only if enough processing happens in Saudi Arabia. This allows duty-free sales in the GCC.
A natural gum that drips from Acacia trees and dries into hard lumps. Used to keep flavours mixed in soft drinks and in sweets and medicines.
The best type of gum arabic, from the Acacia senegal tree.
A cheaper type of gum arabic, from the Acacia seyal tree.
Crushing gum arabic lumps into small even pieces so they dissolve easily.
Turning a liquid into fine powder by spraying it as a mist into hot air; the water evaporates instantly.
The official food-additive code for gum arabic on ingredient labels.
An ingredient that keeps oil and water mixed, like flavours in a soft drink.
Bits that do not dissolve, such as bark and sand, filtered out of gum arabic.
Quality high enough for medicines, made under strict medicine-factory rules (GMP).
Good Manufacturing Practice: strict rules for factories making medicines or supplements.
Certification that food meets Jewish dietary rules. Often required by US buyers.
A large African tree. Its fruit has a dry, tangy powdery pulp sold as a 'superfood'. In Sudan it is called Tabaldi or Gongolez.
Marketing term for foods sold as especially healthy, like baobab powder.
EU approval needed for foods that were not widely eaten in Europe before 1997. Baobab pulp was approved in 2008.
Certified as grown or collected without synthetic chemicals. Sells at a higher price.
Squeezing oil from seeds mechanically without heat, which keeps quality high.
What remains after pressing oil from seeds. A protein-rich animal feed.
Arabic name for hibiscus (roselle). The dried red flower parts make a sour red drink.
The fleshy red part around the hibiscus flower that is dried and sold. Plural: calyces.
Plural of calyx: the dried red parts of the hibiscus flower that are sold.
Hibiscus cut into small even pieces that fit into tea bags.
A concentrated product made by soaking the plant in hot water and removing most of the water.
A thick syrup-like liquid that is diluted with water to make a drink.
The natural red colour in hibiscus. Extracts are priced by how much they contain.
Ready-to-drink: a drink sold in a bottle or can, ready to consume.
An extra tax in Saudi Arabia on certain products, such as sweetened drinks.
Region in eastern Sudan; the main sesame-growing area and market.
Sudan's main seaport on the Red Sea, about 1–2 days by ship from Jeddah.
Large region in central Sudan; main area for gum arabic, hibiscus and baobab. Badly affected by the war.
Region in western Sudan; grows gum arabic, hibiscus and baobab. Hard to access due to the war.
Another country you can buy the same crop from if supply from Sudan stops.
Product that misses the agreed quality standard; usually sold cheaper for other uses.
Being able to show where each batch came from, step by step, back to the area where it was grown.
Extra testing the EU applies to food from certain countries with past safety problems (EU Regulation 2019/1793).
